title: Apple Compote
subtitle: Bramley apples cooked soft with butter and a touch of sugar
excerpt: A quick, deeply flavoured fruit sauce made from Bramley apples, a little sugar, and lemon juice. Ready in twenty minutes and versatile enough to spoon over porridge, pancakes, yoghurt, or ice cream.
sourceNotes: Bramley apple compote is a long-standing British kitchen staple, used as a sauce, filling, and topping across sweet and savoury cooking for over two centuries.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in small portions for up to three months.
recipe.batchNotes: Keeps in the fridge for a week. Freeze in portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Makes up to a week ahead. Store covered in the fridge.

glossaryTerms.definition: Fruit cooked briefly with sugar until soft and syrupy; looser than jam and usually served as a sauce or topping rather than a spread.

content.text: is one of those quietly essential things that transforms a plain bowl of porridge or a stack of pancakes into something worth sitting down for. Bramley apples collapse beautifully under heat, turning from tart firm pieces into a pale, fragrant sauce in under twenty minutes. A little {{unsalted-butter}} butter stirred in at the end gives it body; the {{lemon-juice}} lemon juice keeps the colour bright and lifts the flavour. The main thing to watch is the heat, Bramleys cook fast, so keep the flame low and stir often once they begin to soften.

Peel, core, and roughly chop the {{apple-bramley}} apples into pieces roughly 2 to 3 cm across. They don't need to be uniform, they'll break apart in the pan regardless. Put them straight into the saucepan as you chop; Bramleys oxidise quickly and a rough chop is faster than a neat dice.

Add the {{caster-sugar}} sugar, {{lemon-juice}} lemon juice, and 2 tablespoons of water to the pan. Set over a low-medium heat, stir briefly, and cover with a lid. Leave for five minutes, then lift the lid and stir. The apples will already be releasing liquid. Replace the lid and cook for a further five minutes.

Once the pieces are collapsing, around ten to twelve minutes total, remove the lid and stir more actively. If you want a smooth sauce, mash with the spatula or pass through a sieve. If you prefer texture, leave some chunks intact. Stir in the {{unsalted-butter}} butter until melted and glossy. Taste and adjust the sugar if needed; Bramleys vary quite a lot in tartness depending on the season.
If using {{cinnamon-ground}} cinnamon, stir it in with the butter. Start with a quarter teaspoon, it can overpower Bramley's delicate flavour at full dose.

Serve warm or at room temperature. Spoon over porridge, yoghurt, rice pudding, granola, or British thin pancakes. It's equally good alongside a pork chop or sausages at breakfast, Bramley compote has always worked with savoury as well as sweet. Leftovers keep in a covered jar in the fridge for up to a week. Reheat gently with a splash of water to loosen if it thickens on standing.
Cook uncovered over medium heat for a few minutes to evaporate the excess liquid. Stir constantly so the bottom doesn't catch.
Add a few more drops of lemon juice. Acid is what makes Bramley sing, sugar alone leaves it one-dimensional.
Next time keep the heat lower and add an extra tablespoon of water at the start. The lid matters too, keep it on until the apples have released their own liquid.
